The `WeightTransferEngine` docstring lists RDMA as a TODO; this provides one RDMA option without adding a dependency to vLLM. **Not a duplicate:** searched open PRs and issues for "weight transfer backend", "weight sync RDMA", "RL elastic rollout". Related but different: #52152 (shared-disk backend), #61083 (`sparse_disk` backend), #62557 (per-update source ranks for NCCL), #57374 (XPU torch.distributed), #44994 (fast EP scaling). None adds an RDMA pull backend or handles engines joining or failing during an update. ## Claims - New `--weight-transfer-config '{"backend": "connex"}'`, documented in `docs/training/weight_transfer/connex.md`. - Engines pull each version with one-sided RDMA reads; no communicator group, so engines can join, leave or restart between updates without anyone re-initializing. - Engines that finished pulling serve later pullers (tree fan-out), so the trainer NIC does not serve every engine. - A source dying mid-transfer is survived: the reader switches source and other engines are unaffected. - Cross-node transfer is faster than NCCL broadcast over IPoIB sockets in our setup (caveat below); on a single host NCCL is faster. ## Validation - `pytest tests/distributed/test_weight_transfer.py`: 114 passed, 23 skipped (skips need 2 GPUs or Ray workers) on an A40 host, main d0d681e4. pre-commit on the changed files passes; `ruff check` / `ruff format` (v0.14.0) and `typos` clean. Full `pre-commit run --all-files` not yet run. - End to end through the real entry point (`vllm serve` + `HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient` + `WeightTransferTrainerFactory`): Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, three versions (original, perturbed, original); greedy outputs match the baseline after versions 1 and 3 and differ after version 2. Timings below were measured on vLLM 0.32.0 and not re-run on d0d681e4 (A40, InfiniBand 100 Gb).
Single host, end to end: send_weights() (start + transfer + load + finish), mean of 5 rounds after warm-up | model | `nccl` | `connex` | |---|---|---| | Qwen2.5-0.5B (0.99 GB) | 0.097 s | 0.299 s | | Qwen2.5-1.5B (3.55 GB) | 0.201 s | 0.613 s | | Llama-3-8B (16.1 GB) | 0.798 s | 2.149 s | On one host NCCL uses the PCIe peer path while RDMA reads go through the NIC; this backend is meant for engines on other nodes.

It is not a statement about NCCL over IB in general. Failure case (3.1 GB, 3 receivers): a receiver killed while another was reading from it; the reader switched to the trainer and finished in 0.35 s (0.32-0.42 s without a failure); no other receiver was affected.
## Details - `vllm/distributed/weight_transfer/connex_engine.py`: re-exports `ConnexWeightTransferEngine`, `ConnexTrainerWeightTransferEngine` and their info dataclasses from `connex.rl.vllm_backend`; raises `ImportError` with an install hint on `ModuleNotFoundError` for Connex only. - `factory.py`: lazy registration of `connex` in both factories (imported only when selected). - `receive_weights` loads through `model.load_weights` inside the layerwise reload lifecycle, as the NCCL backend does. 🚀

Hi, thanks for the backend. Some questions:
Advantage
1. Compared with `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n`, what scenario can only Connex handle?
2. When all replicas pull at the same time, does peer fan-out still help? Could you add a same-hardware comparison against NCCL over IB verbs, RDT, and M2N?

 Concerns
1. The trainer holds 2 full-model-sized buffers, and each inference worker keeps one more. What is the measured peak memory on each side, and does the worker buffer eat into KV cache?
2. Each worker pulls the whole model and loads only after the pull finishes. Do you plan per-rank slice pulls and layer-wise pipelining?

Target scenarios
1. What model size, replica count, and parallelism do you run? Do inference nodes scale or get preempted?
2. Are large multi-GPU MoE models like DeepSeek-V4 out of scope?

Thanks for the careful questions. Short answers first, then details. All numbers below are from single runs on A40 GPUs with 100 Gb InfiniBand, on GPUs shared with other tenants, so please read them as indicative.

**Advantage**

1. What only Connex handles, compared with `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n`: a rollout pool whose membership changes while training runs. Both of those backends assume a fixed set of participants known at init (`nccl_m2n` builds one communicator over trainer and workers, and every rank takes part in every reshard; `sharded_rdt` needs the workers to be Ray actors with NIXL). With Connex, an engine that joins later pulls the current version from the trainer or from engines that already hold it, with no group to rebuild; an engine that dies mid-pull does not block the round; and a receiver whose source dies mid-read switches to another source and continues. In a churn run (3.09 GB, three receivers starting 0.5 s apart), one receiver exited while another was reading from it; the reader switched to the trainer and finished in 0.354 s, against 0.32 to 0.42 s in rounds without a failure. A GRPO run with an engine killed during rollouts and a new one joining two steps later completed 256/256 rollouts, with exactly one weight version per step. The other side of this: `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n` move only each worker's slice and handle sharded trainers, and Connex does neither today (see concern 2).

2. When all replicas pull at once, peer fan-out does not help in our current implementation. Fan-out is per finished copy, so receivers that start together all read from the trainer, and peers only serve engines that start later; chunk-level relaying is not implemented. That is the setup of the cross-node numbers below. On the comparison: we have not run NCCL over IB verbs, RDT or M2N on the same hardware. What we measured, transfer only, all receivers starting together, warm rounds:

   | weights | receivers | NCCL broadcast over IPoIB | Connex (connex-rs over IB) |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 0.99 GB | 3 on 2 nodes | 0.611 s | 0.394 s |
   | 3.09 GB | 3 on 2 nodes | 1.949 s | 1.192 s |
   | 16.06 GB | 2 | 5.821 s | 3.334 s |

   The NCCL column is NCCL over IPoIB sockets (`NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1`), because NCCL over IB verbs failed at the first collective in that pod image. So this is **not** a comparison with NCCL over IB verbs, and I would expect NCCL over verbs to close most or all of that gap. On one node NCCL is clearly faster: 0.051 s vs 0.21 s for 0.99 GB, since NCCL uses the PCIe peer path and connex-rs reads go through the NIC. End to end through this API on one host (one engine, `send_weights()` warm), the `nccl` backend took 0.097 / 0.201 / 0.798 s and `connex` 0.299 / 0.613 / 2.149 s for 0.5B / 1.5B / 8B models. I am happy to run a same-hardware comparison against `nccl` over IB verbs, `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n` if that would help the review; I have not done it yet.

**Concerns**

1. Memory. The trainer side packs the weights into a registered arena and keeps `buffers` of them (default 2, so the trainer can publish version v+1 while engines still read v); `buffers=1` halves that, and we had to use it for the 8B model next to the trainer's model on one A40. Each worker keeps one full-model-sized arena, which also lets it serve as a source for peers. The worker arena is allocated lazily at the first pull, after vLLM has sized the KV cache, so it does not shrink the KV cache; instead it has to fit in the memory vLLM leaves outside `gpu_memory_utilization`, and it can fail with OOM if that headroom is too small. I have not measured peak memory on either side; I can add that measurement. Freeing the worker arena after the load (at the cost of no longer serving peers) is a possible option.

2. Yes, today each TP rank pulls the whole model and loads it only after the pull completes (`load_weights` does the sharding). Per-rank slice pulls and layer-wise pipelining are not implemented. Both would fit the design (the pull is chunked one-sided reads against a manifest), but I have no timeline, and for large TP/EP deployments `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n` are the better fit today.

**Target scenarios**

1. What we have run: Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B and Llama-3-8B sized weights (synthetic for the transfer benchmark), up to three receivers on up to three nodes, TP=1 engines, and a GRPO loop on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with two rollout engines in which one engine was killed and a new one joined. The target is rollout pools that scale or get preempted (spot or shared-cluster capacity), where the pool membership is not fixed between steps.
2. Large multi-GPU MoE models such as DeepSeek-V4 are effectively out of scope for this backend today: pulling the full model per rank with no slicing does not scale to that size, and we have not tested multi-node engines or expert parallelism.

## Claude Code Review

This pull request is from a fork — automated review is disabled. A repository maintainer can comment `@claude review` to run a one-time review.

### 🟡 Changes recommended Two existing registry-wide contract tests fail when the optional Connex package is absent.
1 open issue - [Exclude unavailable Connex from deferred processing tests](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63805#discussion_r4380804698) · New
What changed in this PR Adds Connex as an optional worker- and trainer-side backend in vLLM’s weight-transfer API, supporting RDMA-based transfers for elastic rollout pools without a mandatory dependency. **Changes:** - Lazily registers Connex and re-exports its external engine classes and configuration dataclasses. - Adds tests for factory dispatch and the missing-package installation hint. - Documents installation, configuration, and trainer usage. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | `vllm/​distributed/​weight_transfer/​factory.py` | Registers worker and trainer Connex backends lazily. | | `vllm/​distributed/​weight_transfer/​connex_engine.py` | Re-exports Connex APIs and provides an installation hint. | | `tests/​distributed/​test_weight_transfer.py` | Tests lazy dispatch and missing-package handling. | | `docs/​training/​weight_transfer/​README.md` | Adds Connex to the backend comparison table. | | `docs/​training/​weight_transfer/​connex.md` | Documents RDMA transfer behavior, setup, and usage. |
Review effort: Balanced

Registering this optional backend also adds it to `TestDeferredProcessingContract._engines()` in `tests/distributed/test_weight_transfer.py:1578–1584`. That helper invokes every registered loader and only excludes missing ModelExpress, so without Connex installed, both `test_every_engine_declares_whether_it_defers` and `test_every_engine_can_be_drained` now raise the shim's `ImportError`. Please also exclude `connex` when its package is unavailable so the existing suite still passes without the optional dependency.

Confirmed and fixed in df976dd3. `TestDeferredProcessingContract._engines()` now skips the `connex` backend when the `connex` package is not importable, the same way it skips ModelExpress. Without Connex installed, `test_every_engine_declares_whether_it_defers` and `test_every_engine_can_be_drained` failed with the install-hint ImportError before the change and pass after it; with Connex installed, both still exercise the Connex engine and pass. The branch is also rebased onto current main.

 | [nccl_m2n](m2n.md) | NCCL M2N reshard | Trainer and inference use different sharding layouts |
 | [ModelExpress](modelexpress.md) | ModelExpress version-based transfer | Install immutable published weight versions, including object-storage checkpoints and deltas |
+| [Connex](connex.md) | One-sided RDMA reads with tree fan-out | Elastic rollout pools where engines join, leave or fail during updates |
 
 ## Quickstart

@@ -0,0 +1,93 @@
+# Connex Engine
+
+The `connex` weight transfer engine pulls each published weight version with
+one-sided RDMA reads (GPUDirect when available) from the trainer or from
+inference engines that already hold that version. It is maintained in
+[Connex](https://github.com/HeterInfra/connex) and re-exported by vLLM, like
+the [ModelExpress](modelexpress.md) backend.
+
+## When to Use Connex
+
+- The rollout pool is elastic: inference engines join, leave or fail between
+  or during weight updates, and a membership change should not require
+  re-forming a communicator group.
+- One trainer feeds many inference engines across nodes, and the trainer's
+  NIC should not serve every engine: engines that finished pulling serve the
+  next ones (tree fan-out).
+- An engine that dies while others are pulling from it must not stall the
+  update: readers switch to another source and finish.
+
+For a fixed set of engines on a healthy network, [NCCL](nccl.md) broadcast
+remains the simplest choice.
+
+## How It Works
+
+1. The trainer packs its weights into one registered buffer, publishes it as
+   the next version and records the version in the Connex weight registry
+   (a small HTTP service that tracks members, versions and who holds each
+   version).
+2. `update_weights` on each worker asks the registry for a source of that
+   version and reads the buffer in chunks with one-sided reads. A read that
+   fails (source died or left) is retried from another source; reads are
+   idempotent byte ranges.
+3. The worker loads the received tensors with `model.load_weights` inside the
+   layerwise reload lifecycle (`start_weight_update` / `finish_weight_update`),
+   then registers itself as a holder of the version so later pullers can read
+   from it.
+
+vLLM's `connex_engine.py` re-exports the engine and its init/update
+dataclasses from `connex.rl.vllm_backend`.
+
+## Inference Side
+
+Install Connex and its RDMA data plane, connex-rs, on every worker (see the
+Connex README for building connex-rs against the host's UCX):
+
+```bash
+uv pip install "connex-ai[rs]"
+```
+
+```bash
+VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1 vllm serve my-model \
+    --weight-transfer-config '{"backend": "connex"}'
+```
+
+### `ConnexWeightTransferInitInfo`
+
+| Field | Default | Description |
+| ----- | ------- | ----------- |
+| `registry_url` | required | URL of the Connex weight registry. |
+| `member` | host and pid | Logical id prefix of this engine in the registry. |
+| `transport` | `"connex-rs"` | Data plane; `"local"` is an in-process transport for tests. |
+| `chunk_bytes` | 64 MiB | Size of one read. |
+
+### `ConnexWeightTransferUpdateInfo`
+
+| Field | Default | Description |
+| ----- | ------- | ----------- |
+| `version` | latest | Version to install. Older versions are not kept; an engine asked for an older version installs the latest. |
+
+## Trainer Side
+
+```python
+from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer import (
+    HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient,
+    ModuleSource,
+    WeightTransferTrainerFactory,
+)
+from vllm.distributed.weight_transfer.connex_engine import ConnexTrainerInitInfo
+
+engine = WeightTransferTrainerFactory.trainer_init(
+    init_info=ConnexTrainerInitInfo(rank=0, registry_url="http://registry:29700"),
+    client=HTTPVLLMWeightSyncClient("http://inference:8000"),
+    source=ModuleSource(model),
+)
+for step in range(num_steps):
+    train_step(model)
+    engine.send_weights()
+```
+
+The Connex package also provides the registry service, a client that drives
+many engines and drops the ones that fail instead of failing the round, and a
+rollout router that never mixes weight versions within a request; see its
+documentation.

That helper invokes every registered loader and only excludes missing ModelExpress, so without Connex installed, both `test_every_engine_declares_whether_it_defers` and `test_every_engine_can_be_drained` now raise the shim's `ImportError`. Confirmed and fixed in df976dd3. `TestDeferredProcessingContract._engines()` now skips the `connex` backend when the `connex` package is not importable, the same way it skips ModelExpress. Without Connex installed, `test_every_engine_declares_whether_it_defers` and `test_every_engine_can_be_drained` failed with the install-hint ImportError before the change and pass after it; with Connex installed, both still exercise the Connex engine and pass. Hi, thanks for the backend. Some questions:
Advantage
1. Compared with `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n`, what scenario can only Connex handle?
2. When all replicas pull at the same time, does peer fan-out still help? Could you add a same-hardware comparison against NCCL over IB verbs, RDT, and M2N?

 Concerns
1. The trainer holds 2 full-model-sized buffers, and each inference worker keeps one more. What is the measured peak memory on each side, and does the worker buffer eat into KV cache?
2. Each worker pulls the whole model and loads only after the pull finishes. Do you plan per-rank slice pulls and layer-wise pipelining?

Target scenarios
1. What model size, replica count, and parallelism do you run? Do inference nodes scale or get preempted?
2. Are large multi-GPU MoE models like DeepSeek-V4 out of scope?

Thanks for the careful questions. Short answers first, then details. All numbers below are from single runs on A40 GPUs with 100 Gb InfiniBand, on GPUs shared with other tenants, so please read them as indicative.

**Advantage**

1. What only Connex handles, compared with `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n`: a rollout pool whose membership changes while training runs. Both of those backends assume a fixed set of participants known at init (`nccl_m2n` builds one communicator over trainer and workers, and every rank takes part in every reshard; `sharded_rdt` needs the workers to be Ray actors with NIXL). With Connex, an engine that joins later pulls the current version from the trainer or from engines that already hold it, with no group to rebuild; an engine that dies mid-pull does not block the round; and a receiver whose source dies mid-read switches to another source and continues. In a churn run (3.09 GB, three receivers starting 0.5 s apart), one receiver exited while another was reading from it; the reader switched to the trainer and finished in 0.354 s, against 0.32 to 0.42 s in rounds without a failure. A GRPO run with an engine killed during rollouts and a new one joining two steps later completed 256/256 rollouts, with exactly one weight version per step. The other side of this: `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n` move only each worker's slice and handle sharded trainers, and Connex does neither today (see concern 2).

2. When all replicas pull at once, peer fan-out does not help in our current implementation. Fan-out is per finished copy, so receivers that start together all read from the trainer, and peers only serve engines that start later; chunk-level relaying is not implemented. That is the setup of the cross-node numbers below. On the comparison: we have not run NCCL over IB verbs, RDT or M2N on the same hardware. What we measured, transfer only, all receivers starting together, warm rounds:

   | weights | receivers | NCCL broadcast over IPoIB | Connex (connex-rs over IB) |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 0.99 GB | 3 on 2 nodes | 0.611 s | 0.394 s |
   | 3.09 GB | 3 on 2 nodes | 1.949 s | 1.192 s |
   | 16.06 GB | 2 | 5.821 s | 3.334 s |

   The NCCL column is NCCL over IPoIB sockets (`NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1`), because NCCL over IB verbs failed at the first collective in that pod image. So this is **not** a comparison with NCCL over IB verbs, and I would expect NCCL over verbs to close most or all of that gap. On one node NCCL is clearly faster: 0.051 s vs 0.21 s for 0.99 GB, since NCCL uses the PCIe peer path and connex-rs reads go through the NIC. End to end through this API on one host (one engine, `send_weights()` warm), the `nccl` backend took 0.097 / 0.201 / 0.798 s and `connex` 0.299 / 0.613 / 2.149 s for 0.5B / 1.5B / 8B models. I am happy to run a same-hardware comparison against `nccl` over IB verbs, `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n` if that would help the review; I have not done it yet.

**Concerns**

1. Memory. The trainer side packs the weights into a registered arena and keeps `buffers` of them (default 2, so the trainer can publish version v+1 while engines still read v); `buffers=1` halves that, and we had to use it for the 8B model next to the trainer's model on one A40. Each worker keeps one full-model-sized arena, which also lets it serve as a source for peers. The worker arena is allocated lazily at the first pull, after vLLM has sized the KV cache, so it does not shrink the KV cache; instead it has to fit in the memory vLLM leaves outside `gpu_memory_utilization`, and it can fail with OOM if that headroom is too small. I have not measured peak memory on either side; I can add that measurement. Freeing the worker arena after the load (at the cost of no longer serving peers) is a possible option.

2. Yes, today each TP rank pulls the whole model and loads it only after the pull completes (`load_weights` does the sharding). Per-rank slice pulls and layer-wise pipelining are not implemented. Both would fit the design (the pull is chunked one-sided reads against a manifest), but I have no timeline, and for large TP/EP deployments `sharded_rdt` and `nccl_m2n` are the better fit today.

**Target scenarios**

1. What we have run: Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B and Llama-3-8B sized weights (synthetic for the transfer benchmark), up to three receivers on up to three nodes, TP=1 engines, and a GRPO loop on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with two rollout engines in which one engine was killed and a new one joined. The target is rollout pools that scale or get preempted (spot or shared-cluster capacity), where the pool membership is not fixed between steps.
2. Large multi-GPU MoE models such as DeepSeek-V4 are effectively out of scope for this backend today: pulling the full model per rank with no slicing does not scale to that size, and we have not tested multi-node engines or expert parallelism.
